concepts.decision: Approve the process when it assigns accountable roles, activation criteria, communications, dependencies, recovery objectives, and exercise evidence.
concepts.definition: The governed sequence that converts an approved recovery strategy into declaration, notification, assessment, restoration, validation, business acceptance, and return-to-normal activities.
concepts.failureExample: An unowned or untested process produces delayed escalation, conflicting actions, or restoration that cannot be accepted safely.
concepts.label: Disaster Recovery Process

concepts.decision: Declare when verified impact, scope, recovery-objective risk, and designated authority meet the plan’s activation threshold.
concepts.definition: An authorized decision that a disruptive event meets predefined criteria for activating DR governance and recovery resources.
concepts.failureExample: Ambiguous authority or thresholds delay escalation or trigger costly recovery without sufficient evidence.
concepts.label: DR Declaration

concepts.decision: Assign roles before disruption; validate contactability, authority, dependencies, and handoffs in exercises.
concepts.definition: Named primary and alternate responsibilities for technical recovery, business decisions, facilities, security, communications, suppliers, and safety.
concepts.failureExample: A generic team list leaves essential decisions or handoffs unowned when a primary person or network is unavailable.
concepts.label: DR Roles

concepts.decision: Staff the team for the affected services, skills, alternates, supplier dependencies, and safe working conditions.
concepts.definition: The coordinated people who execute technical and business recovery tasks under the assigned recovery authority.
concepts.failureExample: Insufficient skills, absent alternates, or uncoordinated teams can restore components while leaving the service unusable.
concepts.label: Recovery Team

concepts.decision: Use approved messages, owners, cadence, escalation paths, and alternate channels appropriate to the event and audience.
concepts.definition: Controlled, audience-specific communications that keep staff, leaders, customers, suppliers, and authorities informed using resilient channels.
concepts.failureExample: Unverified or inconsistent messages create unsafe actions, regulatory exposure, or loss of stakeholder trust.
concepts.label: Crisis Communications

concepts.decision: Assess before selecting restoration actions; preserve evidence and update scope as facts change.
concepts.definition: A rapid, evidence-based determination of affected people, facilities, systems, data, identities, dependencies, and recovery-option viability.
concepts.failureExample: Restoring on unverified assumptions can spread compromise, overlook dependencies, or choose an unavailable alternate strategy.
concepts.label: Damage Assessment

concepts.decision: Train before an event and refresh after role, system, supplier, or plan changes; verify with exercises.
concepts.definition: Role-specific preparation that enables people to execute recovery procedures, communications, safety actions, and decision handoffs.
concepts.failureExample: Reading a plan does not demonstrate that personnel can coordinate safely under time pressure.
concepts.label: DR Training

concepts.decision: Record observed versus expected results, assign owner/due date/evidence, then retest material changes.
concepts.definition: Evidence-supported findings from events or exercises that lead to owned corrective actions, plan updates, and retests.
concepts.failureExample: Closing an exercise with an attendance record or unowned notes repeats the same readiness gap.
concepts.label: DR Lessons Learned

concepts.decision: Document authority limits, alternates, business acceptance roles, and escalation paths before disruption.
concepts.definition: The delegated decision right to activate DR, commit resources, accept service restoration, manage exceptions, and end recovery status.
concepts.failureExample: A technical team must not silently substitute for business acceptance or commit resources outside its authority.
concepts.label: Recovery Authority

misconceptions.claim: The technical team can declare and prioritize DR alone.
misconceptions.correction: Technical evidence informs the decision, but business authority and continuity priorities determine which services and risks are accepted.

misconceptions.claim: A mass email is a crisis communication plan.
misconceptions.correction: A plan needs authenticated channels, fallbacks, approval, audience-specific content, confidentiality, and tested contact ownership.

outcome: Given a disruptive event, coordinate declaration, response, personnel, communications, assessment, training, and lessons ownership without confusing technical recovery with business acceptance.

sections.body: A DR process translates criteria into an accountable declaration, notification, assessment, response, recovery, and transition sequence. Define who can declare, what evidence or thresholds trigger escalation, which services and dependencies are prioritized, where decisions are recorded, and how emergency access and changes are governed. Response may include life safety, stabilization, containment, alternate processing, supplier coordination, and preservation of evidence. The process should support incomplete information without allowing every team to make conflicting recovery decisions.
keyPoints: Declaration authority and activation criteria should be defined before an event.
Technical and business priorities must be reconciled through a documented decision authority.
Emergency actions still need traceability, access control, and later review.
sections.title: Declare the event and establish control

sections.body: Assign recovery, technical, business, facilities, communications, supplier, security, and safety responsibilities with primary and alternate contacts. Communication methods should account for unavailable networks, confidentiality, authentication, message approval, stakeholder needs, regulators, customers, and staff welfare. Training and awareness make plans executable: people need role practice, contact updates, decision authority, safe work instructions, and escalation routes. Capture lessons from exercises and events with owners and deadlines rather than relying on a retrospective conversation.
keyPoints: A contact list is not a communication plan unless channels and fallbacks are tested.
Personnel safety and role clarity constrain what recovery actions are acceptable.
Training evidence should show that designated people can perform their decisions, not only that they received a document.
sections.title: Coordinate people, communication, and readiness

options.feedback: Changed fact: The primary crisis bridge is unavailable, and a supplier requests privileged credentials by email to accelerate recovery. Why this answer fails: “Reuse the original conclusion because the overall control family is unchanged” does not account for that changed condition. Corrected consequence: Use the defined declaration criteria, record the uncertainty, activate the recovery authority, and obtain the business priority decision while technical teams assess dependencies. Repair target: Decision recomputed — Use the approved out-of-band channel, verify supplier identity and authority, issue bounded emergency access through the controlled process, and record the decision. Pressure and unavailable systems do not remove the need for authenticated communication and least privilege.
